drapeaux.note: The phrases quoted from Paré ("the year one thousand five hundred thirty-six," "venomousness," "my oil failed me") are translated from the 16th-century French as given in the entry; no published English translation was retrieved (original not retrieved).

titre: When Ambroise Paré Ran Out of Boiling Oil
accroche: At the Susa Pass, a surgeon who has run out of boiling oil dresses wounds with an egg digestive, then goes back to see his wounded in the morning
contenu_vulgarise:
At the Susa Pass, in the army sent to Piedmont, a surgeon has never yet seen an arquebus wound treated. He knows the remedy from the books: boiling oil, poured into the wound. In the middle of the treatment, the oil runs short.

## What Paré Reads, What He Does

The account is Paré's own, in his *Discours premier sur le fait des harquebusades* (First Discourse on the Matter of Arquebus Wounds). He places the episode "in the year one thousand five hundred thirty-six," in the service of Montejan; the *Encyclopædia Universalis* dates the battle of the Susa Pass to 1537, and this entry does not settle the matter. Paré writes that he had read in Jean de Vigo that gunshot wounds partake of "venomousness" because of the powder, and that they must be cauterized with elder oil (sambuc), boiling, mixed with a little theriac. He applies this remedy, like the other surgeons, to the wounded brought to him.

Then "my oil failed me." He has to apply instead a digestive made of egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine. At night, he sleeps badly: he fears finding dead of poisoning in the morning the wounded he has not cauterized. He gets up early to visit them.

## What He Finds in the Morning

Those who received the digestive feel little pain, with no inflammation or swelling, and have rested fairly well. Those who received the boiling oil have fever, great pain, swelling, and inflammation around their wounds. Paré then decides never again to burn arquebus-wounded men in this way.

## The Shift

This is not a trial. Paré gives neither the number of wounded, nor how they were divided, nor their severity. The text we read is moreover late: Malgaigne, his 1840 editor, notes that this discourse appears to date from 1575. The force of the scene lies elsewhere: a practitioner who doubts a remedy, and who goes back to see his patients as soon as chance supplies him with a comparison.

The rest of the text shows a surgeon still caught up in the remedies of his time. In Turin, Paré courts for nearly two and a half years a surgeon renowned for treating arquebus wounds, in order to obtain his "balm." The recipe calls for two young dogs, a pound of earthworms, two pounds of lily oil, Venice turpentine, and eau-de-vie: the dogs are boiled alive in the oil until the flesh leaves the bones, the worms, first killed in white wine, are cooked in the same oil until they are dry. The surgeon who gives up boiling oil on the strength of what he has seen thus goes on to adopt a balm whose recipe comes to him from a colleague.

repere.texte: Paré writes that he had read in Jean de Vigo (Book I of Wounds in General, chapter 8) that gunshot wounds partake of venomousness because of the powder, and that they must be cauterized with sambuc oil mixed with a little theriac.
repere.source: A. Paré, Discours premier sur le fait des harquebusades, in Œuvres complètes, ed. J.-F. Malgaigne, vol. II, 1840

carte.punch: Out of boiling oil, a surgeon notices that his wounded are doing better.
carte.idee: For lack of oil, Paré dresses his arquebus-wounded with a digestive of egg, rose, and turpentine. In the morning, they suffer less than the wounded cauterized with boiling oil. He gives up the method, without having run a trial.

quiz.question: What leads Paré to give up boiling oil?
choix: An order from a superior after the complaints of the wounded
Reading a recent treatise that condemned Jean de Vigo
His comparison, in the morning, of the wounded treated with oil and with the digestive
A report by the physicians of the Paris faculty
quiz.explication: For lack of oil, Paré treated some of the wounded with the digestive, and the next day he finds less pain and inflammation in them than in those who were cauterized. No order, recent treatise, or opinion of the faculty is mentioned in his account; it was Vigo who prescribed the oil.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Paré fear, at night, finding wounded men dead in the morning?
choix: He believed the powder poisoned the wounds, as Vigo wrote
He knew the egg digestive made gunpowder wounds worse
He lacked bandages to cover all the wounds of the wounded
He had been ordered not to let any wounded man in the camp die
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Paré had read in Vigo that powder makes wounds venomous and that they must be cauterized. Without oil, he therefore fears finding dead of poisoning those he has not cauterized. The digestive does not make it worse according to the morning's findings, and his text mentions neither a lack of bandages nor an order.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the rest of the account show about Paré's break with old remedies?
choix: He now condemns all remedies based on animals
He later obtains a balm made from dogs and earthworms
He definitively gives up war surgery
He gets his method approved by the physicians of Turin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After courting a Turin surgeon for nearly two and a half years, Paré obtains his balm: dogs and earthworms cooked in oil. He therefore does not condemn all animal remedies, and he does not leave war surgery.
